utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T. The Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everyone, and may we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. It's Joanna Korner, Belinda Pidwell, and Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Slobodan Zecevic and Slobodan Cvijetic for Stanisic Defence. Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, Dragan Krgovic for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, before the witness comes back in again, Mr. Zecevic and I did not meet yesterday afternoon, because Mr. Zecevic still wants to consider the position in respect of what is to be done about the document saga.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Package of 108?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly the package. He may -- the witness may start this afternoon he may not, I'm not sure about that. However, I am afraid it occurred to me yesterday that because of the time constraints, I omitted a number of documents that were on the list for the present witness, Mr. Krulj. Basically because they amount to much of the same thing, you remember the first few documents I showed you were communications up to republic level or between the SJBs and the CSB. But the difficulty is that I don't know where we are at the moment on this question of whether we can put in remaining documents, for example, if we can't come to some sort of an agreement about communications and the number of documents we have showing communications as a bar table motion. If we can, then I don't need to go back over the others. But if we can't, then I do. And these are all virtually identical. I omitted, for example, 65 ter 939, 960, 963 because, as I say, my view was until we had this discussion yesterday that I could put them in through a bar table motion, if I had to. Now, if that's an agreed way of dealing with it, then I can just continue with this question of the diary today. But if not, then I have to go back and put the other documents in through this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, are we talking right now about the 108 documents we ruled upon yesterday and you tried to get an agreement with?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no, no, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay, then I misunderstood you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Complete misunderstanding, Your Honour. Until Your Honours gave the ruling yesterday which relates to the next witness, I hadn't appreciated or not properly appreciated the way that Your Honours want to approach the admission of documents. And in dealing with Mr. Krulj, I omitted from the list that everybody had something like 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 documents that simply showed communication having put in one or two of them as examples on the basis either that at some stage we will be able to reach agreement with the Defence about the communication documents, or if we couldn't reach agreement, in other words, if it's not accepted that we hold in our possession a large number of documents relating simply to communication, then those documents that I did not put in with the witness because of the time constraints we would put in as exhibits through a bar table motion. But clearly, this witness can talk about them as he has about the others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: He can't?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Of course he can, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He can, yes. But it seems to me it's a complete waste of the Court's time not to mention the Prosecution's valuable time simply to say to him, is this yet another example of a report that went up. And then you know, wait while I ask for it to be admitted. And so because I said two and a half hours -- and can I say all our estimates of how long it would take to get through this case were based on an obviously erroneous understanding that a lot of documents would go in through a bar table motion. So what I'm asking now is whether as I have this witness here, is it Your Honours' ruling that I want to get these documents, the other communication documents in I have to take him through those as well? That's what I'm asking. Instead of simply, as I say, at the end putting them in through a bar table motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: A couple of questions before we decide on the issue. First of all, have these documents been disclosed to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, they are all on our list, they are 65 ter documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But I understand that they were not on the list that you intended to show to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no. Sorry, Your Honour, you were sent --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- as were the Defence, a list of documents saying witness ST-202.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you looked at yesterday's transcript, you will note that I went through 65 ter 936, 938, I skipped 939, I put in 959, I skipped 960, -63, -73. Exactly. Because they are just more of the same thing. And as I say, either at some stage during this trial we reach agreement with the Defence about documents relating purely to communications with either the CSB, and there's a firm shaking of the head going on there, or it means we'll have to put the documents in to show the amount of communication that there was. Now, I think it's a waste of time to simply say to this witness, have a look at this documents, this relates to Trebinje. This is another one of the same reports. I was proposing, therefore, to put them all in through a bar table motion, or alternatively, have them all admitted now because they are all -- the ones I've asked him about are all samples which is what you are suggesting from Mr. Djeric.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Every document I've put to him is on that list, there were three extra ones that I haven't got to yet, which I handed in. But every single document on this list that I put to him was on this list. I haven't put anything outside this list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So we are only talking about documents that for reasons of convenience you did not choose to put to this witness while he was here?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And -- right. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Before we rule on it, we would like to hear the position of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I fully understand the position of Ms. Korner, and we are going to be in the same position, so, therefore, we would just like to avoid one thing. I don't think that it's acceptable the second alternative which she proposed, being that witnesses shown one document and then all the others as a similar documents are admitted because, again, we are coming to the situation that these documents will be tested by Defence. So the time that will be -- that would be saved on the Prosecution side will be used by the Defence in the cross-examination. And, therefore, we might then be penalised because we took more time than anticipated but that is only because of the rulings of the Trial Chamber on the admission of the documents. I mean, I need this to be understood fully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: No, I fully appreciate your concerns. But my question is this: Would that be any different if these five or six documents were to be admitted through a bar table motion? You would have the same problem, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, if these documents would be admitted through the bar table motion, we would be, of course, given the opportunity to be heard on the matter, in writing. To respond to the bar table motion. But there is not going to be any more witnesses to test the documents. So, therefore, I think the bar table motion would save time in the ultimate -- at the ultimate level. It will save time of the -- save the Court time by bar table motion, because what it does is that the Prosecution proposes 200 documents, they are obliged to explain the relevance, the authenticity of each and every one, we respond to that, and then Your Honours decide. That is as far as I understood and if Ms. Korner can confirm that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I agree. I mean, I might say it's not a concept that's very familiar to me because it doesn't exist in my jurisdiction, but as I understand it, we put them in, in writing, we explain the relevance and why we want them admitted and we would say in this particular case because of the time constraints we couldn't take the witness through each and every one of them but Your Honour heard this witness. So that's how it would happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: The Chamber's ruling is the following: We will allow these five or six documents that you did not put to this witness to be introduced through a bar table motion, but we stress that we do this on an exceptional basis because we realise that we will be faced with the same issue again and again and again on other matters and maybe even on this matter, the matter of communication. So we will -- we will reserve our position to deal with it, you know, on a case-by-case basis. But we do think and we do agree with the parties that it will save court time if we can have them agreed as -- if we can have them introduced, sorry, through a bar table motion. But again, the concern of the Chamber is, in perspective, that we would wish to be careful not to be too generous in admitting a very large portion of documentary evidence through a bar table motion at the end because the experience is that once we get to the end of the trial it will be unmanageable. So for these documents, we will admit them and then next time it happens we'll take a particular position.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Yes, can I just say to Your Honours, it is something that's going to come up over and over again, I'm afraid. And it would be -- we can obviously deal with it on another occasion because we ought to get on, but it is something really that we ought to be able to sort out once and for all because case-by-case basis it's just going to take up time. Can I say, for example, that there's a witness coming who is going to deal with Sanski Most documents where if I had to put every single one that is relevant through him, he will be here for days, he would be on videolink for days actually, so I'm just saying, that's what's going to happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yet, if the parties do reach some sort of an agreement on this, on how it to deal with the documentary evidence that only shows one single aspect, namely that communication, for instance, just as an example, that communications did take place on a very regular basis between two or three institutions, then I think that might solve at least this problem. Other problems may then arise, but hoping and waiting for a possibly agreement between the parties on this issue we'll prefer that until then we do it deal with it on a case-by-case basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, Your Honours, we discussed that in the pre-trial during the 65 ter conference. We say that the communication is an issue in this case and we -- there is no agreement between us and the Prosecution on that. I said that during the pre-trial phase on the 65 ter conference, and I'm repeating it right now on the record. So there's no possibility of the agreement between us on that particular matter. And I don't -- I fully agree with Ms. Korner. If we are -- if we are faced with this issue on a case-to-case basis, it would mean that Ms. Korner will have to stand up each and every day, each and every -- after each and every witness and say, Your Honours, in consideration of time I omitted these documents, I would -- I propose to offer them through the bar table motion. Then we will have our comments, then Your Honours will be deciding that, and then again we will be using valuable court time. Instead of deciding once and for all what are the rules. Because we would be much more comfortable if we would know what are the rules in presentation of evidence in this case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zecevic. The reason why we were hoping for some sort of an agreement was that by your own admission yesterday, we understood that some sort of contact would be made between the parties in relation to the 108 documents that are coming through the next witness. So this is what led us to believe that there was still some sort of communication going on about this. But your statement today makes it clear that no such agreement will take place and we may reconsider our position. But let me add this: That if the issue of communication is a very central aspect of this trial, then I'm not sure if we serve justice right by having all the evidentiary documentation submitted to us through a bar table motion. Then in fact it might be better to face the music with the witnesses at least in relation to some of the documents, and then face the music, as I say, let's hear it from the witnesses what is the true story about communications according to the witnesses. Because if this is really such a controversial issue, I would be hesitant to have to deal with it in the end purely on the basis of 500 documents that were admitted to us through a bar table motion. That simply isn't a proper way of dealing with such a crucial issue. Then I would rather have it from the witnesses and then we may have to decide on a different way in which we introduce this evidence to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I fully agree with Your Honours. I fully agree with that. What I'm trying to say is, Your Honours, there are issues and issues in this case. The spirit of cooperation that we have with the Office of the Prosecutor is on basis of some of the issues we are able to reach an agreement and we are moving in that direction, which I think should only be positive sign. Now, there are some issues where we definitely cannot, but what I'm trying to -- what I'm trying to find out would be the principle, how are we dealing with the exhibits in general, not -- I somehow, with all due respect, have the feeling that we are -- we are concentrating on certain issues, but we would like to know the overall frame of introduction of the evidence in this case. The clear situation so we can plan in advance and we know which way and which actions to take. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Can I try -- I would like to try to explain the concern of the Trial Chamber and how we thought that eventually we could deal with it. And I take a totally stupid example to avoid to get you an example that is in issue. If there are 100 documents to which one of the parties wants to prove that Mr. So-and-so, and it has -- all documents concern one sort of kind of a meeting in a municipality, and what one tries to prove is that Mr. So-and-so was not present at all those meetings, but in those documents there is a lot more than only the presence or the non-presence of that person. So at that moment, they could come in as a whole, as a bundle. If we restrain the evidence to the fact that Mr. So-and-so is present or is not present. And there you could agree upon that those documents come only in with the purpose of proving that specific fact and all the rest we can ignore. That's how we were trying to settle this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, that is entirely acceptable for us. The problem, I think, which is -- which is like the problem which cannot be avoided is that the documents usually do address a couple of different issues. It's not that simple. But, I mean, if it -- if we would be told that the certain documents serve the purpose of establishing this particular aspect only, then we might sit down and talk to the opposing side. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, can I just say one of the problems is, we've been going since quarter past 2.00 now on this subject, and if we do it on a case-by-case basis, it's going to come up every single time, and I echo Mr. Zecevic's desire that we actually have a proper system set in place as opposed to dealing with things by case-by-case basis. And the second thing is this: That our estimates of time and the time that you've given us were not based in any sense, at least not from our point of view or indeed I believe from the Defence's point of view, of having to put every document we wanted exhibited to the witness. It just takes a very very long time. And documents, as I said yesterday, are the basis of most of the leadership cases. That's what they amount to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, if I may, I think we should stop now this discussion. I think we have fully appreciated your concerns. We have said that for these five or six documents that you would have to put through this witness we will go along with the bar table motion. But the Court will have to think again about how to prove this. Obviously these documents, I suppose, will tend to show that the two accused were well informed of events on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Right. So this is the issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As simple as that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And you are seeking to prove this by putting to us and to the witnesses a big number of documents that would indicate that Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Zupljanin were well informed by way of all these communications and letters and reports and bulletins to them. So when Mr. Zecevic says that he will have no objection to going on, getting on with that and accepting this, then of course the next issue arises about well, what exactly was in those documents because it is not enough to show that communications took place and that a lot of bulletins went up and down. You also have to prove that -- that the two accused were actually informed about some of the crimes that were committed on the ground. And this is where it becomes difficult for the Chamber to have to deal with a very large number of documents that tend to show the commission of crimes exclusively on the basis of a bar table motion. Documents that we are just being given in a huge bundle, hundreds and hundreds of documents that we will then have to sit and read through after the trial and determine, you know, whether we can trust that the two accused were really informed about all of these fantastic things that we now discover in the documents. This is why I'm saying, well, maybe we should think about - and this is what we will do - think about an alternative way of getting at least some of these documents confronted to a witness and have the witnesses' testimony about it. Not all of them necessarily, but at least some of them. And that is what is exactly the way we propose in relation to the 108 documents that the Prosecution says that these 108 documents relate to three different aspects, and the proposal by the Chamber was therefore let's have a couple of documents from each of these three categories and see what they say. And if you assert that all the remaining documents in each category say the same thing or almost the same thing, then we will be willing to admit all of them. But not without having seen at least some of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. May I say, I absolutely agree with you. For example, communications, obviously we are selecting hopefully we have witnesses who will come who are able to speak from their own knowledge of the events in the document or the document themselves, which is why we had Mr. Draganovic with all the Crisis Staff minutes. We would then hope to in some way or another not have to deal with simply what Your Honour rightly refers to as evidence that there was communication as opposed to specific events. The reason we are doing this is because it's clear from Mr. Stanisic's interview with the OTP, and that's why it's such an issue that he rejects communication, he says there was - I'm summarising - but there was a complete breakdown in communication and that's -- we have to deal with that as I said I think before. With regard to the next witness, in fact I said three categories as a rough thing, but we broke it down into some more, we sent those categories I think to Your Honours and to the Trial Chamber. The difficulty there is they fall into the same category in that they are assembly minutes or government minutes but they are not the same. And in particular, the assembly minutes all say different things, and deal with different topics. We broke it down, in fact, into eight categories when we went and did a double-check, which is assembly minutes, Presidency minutes, NSC joint Presidency minutes, NSC minutes, council ministers, government ministers and then documents relating to directly to the witness and a few miscellaneous, so in fact there's a total of eight categories. Now, we were proposing to adopt Your Honours' suggestion or ruling on this matter when it comes to him and simply pick out some examples from each category and then ask for the rest to be admitted as exhibits. So that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And that was the ruling we handed down yesterday exactly in order to try and find a solution to how to deal with this enormous amount of documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly. The same will apply not to the next witness because he is a 92 ter but the one after that. There are two witnesses who can deal with these major documents. Your Honours, that's all I want to say. Perhaps we can get Mr. Krulj back in again and, Your Honours, I'm -- in the light of discussing this about the diary, I'm just going to have to take him through some more entries in the diary. Can I just check, though, that 65 ter number 198, which is the July 11th meeting, was in fact made an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It was admitted as Exhibit P160.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could the witness have the binder back. Thank you. And can we have up on the screen, so we don't waste too much time. 65 ter number 2118. And I cannot tell you anything of B/C/S ... So the B/C/S page will be -- for the next entry will be 26.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Page 26. And in the English it's also page 26.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Krulj, I'm sorry again you've been kept waiting, and let's go back to this diary, and don't worry about who wrote it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If I may have a moment, Ms. Korner. Mr. Krulj, I remind you you are still under oath. Ms. Korner, the comment that you made just before the witness came in, where you said in it the light of the discussion about the diary, I take it you are picking up where we left of off at the adjournment yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, my understanding was that unless I could show that this diary contained meetings about which this witness can speak, I can't have it admitted as an exhibit because the Defence objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: No. In terms of the contents, the Chamber had no difficulty as regards the relevance, and therefore, admissibility on that ground. Our difficulty was a more narrow one, and it had to do with the providence and authenticity of the diary. And you had referred in your submissions yesterday to the fact that our rules of admissibility do not require a signature or proof of authorship for admissibility. But the point -- the concern of the Chamber was that those -- that possibility is not so broad as to allow into evidence a document which, and I'm trying to express what I'm trying to say, I intend no disrespect to counsel on either side and I'm certainly casting no aspersions on the probity of counsel, but the persons -- a document which could have been manufactured by whomever and yet used by the side seeking to rely on it to get it in, if there is no evidence whatever before the Tribunal as to where the document came from therein lies the difficulty. Once that hurdle would have been overcome by the side relying on the document, then the problem as we see it is solved, because as Judge Delvoie would have said yesterday, in terms of the contents itself, there is the clear connection.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, but what I'm -- yes. Firstly, we understood we didn't have to call evidence about the providence of these documents. Therefore, we dispensed with Mr. Mitford-Burgess from our witness list, but we can call evidence to show that we acquired this document from the RS MUP, and I have forgotten where it was now, who provided it to one of our investigators, I believe. So we can say where it comes from, it comes from Trebinje. The point is that it contains entries which we don't have other documentation for of meetings which this witness can say he attended. And it doesn't, in our submission, matter whether we can actually prove who the author was. I suppose it's conceivable that the Republika Srpska MUP may have manufactured this diary, but it seems to be highly improbable. And therefore, the test for its admission is can the witness speak to the contents? Answer, he can. We suggest that under your rules and the rules of this Tribunal it should be admitted as an exhibit and then the weight that's given to it is dependent on what else we can say about the diary. So that's the reason. That's why -- I don't particularly want to take this witness, certainly I'm sure the witness would prefer I'm not going to take him through these rather tedious meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We have no difficulty with the diary being marked for identification at this point, but I've alerted you to what you may have to do at some point down the road.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, you see, all right, Your Honour, again that's something else that hasn't come up before. If there's a challenge to the -- well, there isn't a real challenge to it, it's just that Mr. Zecevic says doesn't know who wrote the diary, full stop. We are going to have to call evidence as to how we acquired the document, we the OTP, I mean. Because if so, I mean, then we will have to put back on to our witness list the investigator in charge of the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, could you assist us on this point. Ms. Korner, as I understand her, is saying that your objection was limited to the fact that the Prosecution to -- to the assertion that the Prosecution hasn't proved the authorship of the diary which as Ms. Korner has pointed out, would not, without more, be sufficient to exclude it. Could we understand clearly what, if any, your challenge is to the admissibility of this diary?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe I was pretty clear yesterday when I made the objection. There are two aspects of this: The Prosecution is stating that this particular diary belongs to a certain person who passed away, and this witness states that this is very unlikely that this diary belongs to that person because the way how it was written. So in my opinion, this is -- this is a valid ground to object to the -- to admission of this document. That's number one. The second -- the second issue that I had was a nexus between this particular witness and then the diary of we don't know who. Despite the fact that the witness may confirm some of the meetings, he can confirm that there has been some of the meetings, but I mean, there are some comments contained in this diary. I mean, obviously we will need to know to at least a certain extent to whom does it -- does it belong at all to the member of MUP? It might be somebody else. Thank you. I hope I was of assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Of course on your last point, the witness has yet to be cross-examined by you, so no doubt you are making a note of that and would explore it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Definitely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So it's the first point with which we must be concerned, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I would definitely cross-examine the witness after.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I -- we don't say -- our theory is that it was written by a particular gentleman because of what is contained in the diary, but we say it doesn't matter whether it was written by this gentleman or some other gentleman within the MUP, and I would ask the witness to confirm that, whoever wrote this diary it's a police type of diary and it's a member of the MUP in Trebinje. So therefore we say as such, and that's clear from the contents of this diary, it's an admissible document. If we can show further who actually wrote it, then it adds to, if you like, the indicia of reliability that Your Honours would be looking for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I think let's get on with it now. In the face of a challenge against the authenticity of this diary, it will, and I'm sure you will appreciate, be difficult for the Chamber to admit it because there is a risk that it may have been manufactured by someone completely different. So I don't see that there's any way around the hard way, namely, to confront the witness, this witness, with the aspects in the diary which you wish to have confirmed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's what I was starting to do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes, that's why I say let's get on with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Sorry about this, Mr. Krulj. First of all, you've had a chance on a number of occasions to look through the diary; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Whoever wrote that diary, and don't worry about whether it's Cuk or somebody else, in your view was this gentleman who wrote the diary a member of the MUP in Trebinje?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And in that diary, are there meetings recorded which you to your knowledge attended?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are some parts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Let's try and take a selection of those meetings. First of all, can you look in your divider -- sorry, your bundle behind divider 28 and go to the page number you can see on the screen 02971419. And in the English it's page 26. Now, this records a meeting with the SJB chiefs on the 10th of July, 1992. And the agenda is proposed candidates for the national security service and preparations for a working meeting in Belgrade. The following day, and you've already looked at it, was the 11th of July where the big meeting in Belgrade was held. Do you remember talking about that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which page?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, in the B/C/S -- in the Serbian language you will see at the top 02971419. Tab 28, I'm sorry. If you go to tab 28, please. And on the top you will see, it's about ten pages, it's got the number on the top 02971419.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not divider 28.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you have a look at the screen?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you see there Trebinje, 10th of July, 1992. Right.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Meeting with the SJB chiefs -- meeting with the SJB chiefs agenda proposed candidates for the national security service, preparations for working meeting in Belgrade, use of the special unit. Now, the meeting in Belgrade, was that the one that you attended on the 11th of July that we looked at yesterday?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but not this meeting. Listen, there was Gacko, Bileca, Nevesinje, Stolac, and Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but sorry, it says, Meeting with the SJB chiefs, Bileca and Gacko, this is candidates, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see it from this text, and I think that I've told you earlier that I did not attend the meeting on the day prior to it because this was one day before the meeting in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah. And it says, Departure from Trebinje at 700 hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, can we go to the next page, please, in the English, 27. And in the B/C/S, it's the next page as well, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Departure from Trebinje at 0700 hours by minibus. Did you go in a minibus from Trebinje to the meeting on the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think we went in a minibus but in a regular vehicle. We never had any kind of a minibus.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Did you go with Mr. Savic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But not by minibus?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You left -- did you leave from Trebinje at 0700 hours?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. You see apparently at that meeting there was an order that Muslim and Croat judges be arrested and that interviews be conducted. Do you remember Muslim and Croat judges being arrested?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is from the meeting held a day prior to that, and I told you that I did not attend that meeting, so I don't remember. It just carries on on the following page the text concerning the meeting on the 10th of July.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, can we go then, please, to the 15th of July. If you didn't attend a meeting, would you send your commander to the meeting?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that anybody attended. You can see the list of attendees. Their names are written at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but it says, Meeting -- never mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Rather than argue with this you about this. Can you go to the 15th of July, 02971423, which is page 30 in both the English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Again it's headed "Trebinje, 15th of July meeting with SJB chiefs, agenda tasks resulting from the working meeting of the SRBH MUP held in Belgrade." And miscellaneous. Did you attend that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 15th of July, 1992; right? How many items on the agenda are there?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Two apparently. Sorry, should be in front of you.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have another one here that was opened in front of me where there are 18 items on the agenda, 423 Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. It's item 1. Can you look at the screen. I just want to know, we've been through -- we went through this in the interview. Is this a meeting that you attended?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Can I just ask you, I know it's a long time ago, you went through this last time, seven, "Securing the Prisoners." Which prisoners were being discussed there?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this meeting followed the meeting in Belgrade. We read the conclusions, and it should have been conveyed to all the chiefs of the public security stations, and by the time we returned, of course, a meeting was scheduled, and it proceeded according to the items on the agenda of the 11th of July, all of them were conveyed to the chiefs of the stations. There were discussion about protecting the border crossings, about the units allocated for protection that were deployed in these camps or collection centres. So everything that is in the agenda of the meeting from Belgrade was also conveyed at this meeting here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I see. All right. So that's what it refers to, is it? All right. Can we move on then, please, to the 17th of July, page 35.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we look there, we can see that under item 3, Bileca, we see Ljubinje, Krunic, and Mihic. Who were they?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: What it says here underneath the order accompanying the report, item 3, all of these are members of the national security or the state security. I don't recall this meeting. Ratko Lare [phoen] and Koprivica, Mirko were in Trebinje; Zoran Vidakovic in Gacko; Krunic and Mihic in Ljubinje; and Bozo Grahovac in Nevesinje. These are former SDB [as interpreted] employees, and this is related to the organising of the national securities sector. But this has nothing to do with us, or with public security. I think that I did not attend this meeting because that has nothing to do with the stations. This is a separately organised unit or service.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But it says meeting of SJB chiefs and commanders. Wasn't this about candidates for the national security service?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible, it doesn't say here who attended, but it doesn't seem logical to me for the public security station chiefs to be discussing candidates for employees of a different service, particularly of the national or state type of service. This is some kind of professional leadership or expert drafting. I'm using the word "expert" in quotes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you move it to the 31st of July, page 41.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We see there that there's an overview of the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Under 2, the establishment of [B/C/S spoken] unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly, did you attend this meeting? We can see there is a report from Ljubinje on the next page, 42?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I probably did. Either I did or the commander did. I cannot recall the date, but let's say that I did. Somebody did attend in any case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: On the formation of the special purpose unit, that's at page 44, if you go over, sir, to -- I think you'll find it at page 0 -- no, I can't find anything more. But do you remember the discussions about this formation of the special unit?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do because it was agreed at the meeting in Belgrade to abolish all so-called Specijalna Jedinica units in the area of the stations and the centre to prevent their activities and to form a Specijalna unit as part of the brigade under the brigade command and that we from the security centre should try to secure accommodation for that unit and to provide it with maximum support in terms of the most -- the best trained and the most junior cadre trained for police tasks and we actually completed that in late 1992 or 1993. Early 1993 when this unit was actually formed. I don't recall the exact time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we move now to the 20th --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, may we have a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, right in the beginning, and Mr. Krgovic as well, of course, right in the beginning of his testimony today, it was the first question Ms. Korner asked. First of all -- wait just a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. If the witness can confirm that it was somebody from the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes. With this -- with this firm yes of the witness, is your challenge still standing?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, my challenge -- my challenge was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The first one, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The first one -- well, the first challenge was concerning the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Authenticity.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Concerning the alleged -- that the alleged owner of this diary is late Cuk. That was the position of the Prosecution. Now the witness have confirmed that it must have been somebody from the SUP, so therefore we know that. And I didn't file any -- I didn't raise and file any objections any more because I think -- but obviously these things have to be established. That was the point of my objection before. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, we think that this is enough for you to -- not to continue this line of questioning just to prove the authenticity of the document. So we can accept it as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. Okay. Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Krulj, we needn't go through this rather tedious exercise. Can I ask you then finally --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- one last document on the screen, although, I don't think you've seen it before. We didn't show it to you. It's 65 ter number 1792. And that diary, I hope is going to be made an exhibit now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P168, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't think that can be it, sorry. Is that the first page? Yes, sorry, the first page. You are on the second page now. First page in English, please. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is a report to the minister of the interior from the CSB in Trebinje dated the 13th of January, 1993, and it's a report on the work between the 4th of April and the 31st of December 1992. Was this a standard report that would be sent, Mr. Krulj?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's a standard report. We are talking about the end of the year and the start period is the 4th of April. That's when the ministry was formed, so I assumed that that is an annual report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I just want to ask you a couple of questions, then, about the contents of this. In paragraph 3 it starts: "Before this the minister of the interior of the government of the SAO Herzegovina had organised meetings of Serbian staff from this area at which plans were adopted for the engagement of the police in the event of a war or imminent threat of war." Did you attend any such meetings?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm not aware of this report either, and I had no part in its drafting for sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, no, if we go to the end, it's actually stamped.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go to the last page, please, page 5 in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: By Krsto Savic and signed by somebody on his behalf apparently.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We've got both in B/C/S. Can we have the English up, please. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's signed for him. This is a Z or an L in the Cyrillic script. What would you like to know about the signature? It's not Krsto Savic's signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's somebody signing on his behalf, but does that appear to you to be an official stamped and signed report?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, yes, there are no markings, it's true, but, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I want to go back, please, I'm sorry, just for one moment, to the first page both in the English and the B/C/S to the last paragraph in January 1992. Last paragraph on the B/C/S page as well, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "In January 1992 the Special Police unit was already undergoing training in barracks in Bileca and was ready to carry out the most complex tasks." Did you know about a Special Police unit undergoing training in barracks in Bileca?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday that it was formed in what way, I think this happened before, before 1992 because the war began on the 1st of October 1991 and we have the preparations in January. But I think that this unit existed before January 1992. That's my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And do you know what the most complex tasks were that it carried out?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I heard was that it was helping at the front in certain areas in the Dubrovnik and the Mostar theatres. That's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you mean just straight engaged in combat?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But would combat be described, in your experience, as a complex task?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most complex one, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Yes, all right. Thank you, Mr. Krulj.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may that be made an exhibit. It's on our 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P169, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Krulj, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I note the time, I don't know if you want me to start or?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, we have five minutes. [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, my microphone wasn't on. I was saying that you have five minutes before the scheduled break.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I heard you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could the witness [sic] provide this binder for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krulj, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I am going to ask you before we begin to speak slowly and to make a pause before you begin responding to my question so that the interpreters could interpret my question completely as well as your answer. Please, we speak the same language so usually what happens is that we often overlap and then the interpreters have difficulties to follow.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Krulj, I'm going to go through your particulars quickly. You were employed at the centre of the security services in Mostar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: At the time, I'm talking about the period prior to the 1990s, you were one of the best educated policeman in the Herzegovina area?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you take it that way, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: During the examination-in-chief, you said that you were overseeing and monitoring the activities of the police on the territory of Herzegovina up until 1989; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from 1986, this is actually a part of the job description of the police inspector.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Then in the 1990s, you were transferred to work on defence preparations in the Ljubinje SRB -- SJB?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us very briefly, we have a couple of minutes, explain to us what does that mean, defence tasks in the public security station very briefly?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every public security station in Bosnia-Herzegovina before the war --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just slowly.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were categorisations of the posts which -- and one of the posts was the desk officer for defence preparations. And it was his job to man the reserve forces adequately which were provided for under the regulations of the internal operations of the ministry. So a station could not have a larger number of the reserve members than that provided for under the Ministry of the Interior regulations. Part of the duties of this officer were replenishment, regular training, training of the reserve forces, conduct of certain tactical or exercises in the field, which provided for the use of the reserve forces of the police. Where I worked in my town we had about an 80 strong reserve force. These were militarily-fit-for-service men who were vetted in certain ways, checked if they had a criminal record or not, and this was -- there was also a Special Police force unit within this unit which was made up partially of active reserves -- active forces and then the reserve forces. Yesterday --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you here, I'm going to lead you through this then we will cover the grounds more quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, we are going to make a break and then we will continue when we come back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We will resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, while the witness is ushered in, I would like just to announce that we are joined with Mr. O'Sullivan as part of the Stanisic Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krulj, let us summarise what we have just talked about. In 1989 you transferred to work at the SJB Ljubinje as an officer for defence preparation tasks for that SJB?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, these defence preparations were planned in accordance with the duty of all state and other social organs in the former Yugoslavia in accordance with the Law on National Defence?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is to say, that all entities, state organs, social organs, companies, schools, all of these entities had a duty to have a defence plan and act in accordance with it, including the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And as for the Ministry of the Interior, it was an administrative organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please make sure that you make a break between question and answer, please. Let me just ask you this first: In accordance with these mandatory provisions of the Law on National Defence, was there also an order on implementing the plan for defence preparations on the part of the Ministry of Interior of Bosnia and Herzegovina back in 1989 when you were performing those duties?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the transcript, I said 1989 page 32, line 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I will now show to you the order of the MUP of Republika Srpska of the 15th May, 1992 this is 65 ter number 126.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please see it on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In your binder, it should be under number 1. Please open it. Just press on it. You also have that document on the monitor. Please tell me, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we received a lot of documents, and I think we received this one, and I do recognise it. I can't quote the entire content though, but, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please look at the last page, the signature. Do you recognise the signature of the minister, Mico Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that is his signature, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please look at the document, take a couple of minutes, if you need, I wish to ask you whether this document dated 15th of May 1992 was in any way different from other documents that you normally came across at the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1989?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not different.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So this means that this document, the content of this document is identical to other documents that are -- were used for defence preparations in the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina before 1992, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please look at this at page 2, item 7, last line. It says here: "While carrying out combat operation, the units of the ministry shall be subordinated, shall be resubordinated to the command of the armed forces. However, the ministry units shall be under the direct command of certain ministry officials."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. I think we have a problem with the document in English. We have a completely different document on the right-hand side. I asked for 65 ter 126 to be put on our screens. Could we see page 2, item 7 of that document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Krulj, this means, and you can correct me if I'm wrong, that in case where combat operations are carried out, in case where there is a war, MUP units are mobilised and placed under the command of armed forces, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's how it was before the war, and unfortunately the war erupted, and I had to do it during the war, but it was done in the same way before the war as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When they say here that the ministry units shall be under the direct command of certain ministry officials, do they mean that a unit in an organised fashion together with a commander goes to positions and that the unit commander is then subordinated to the military officer at the location where combat operations are to be carried out, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So that means that this commander of a police unit which is resubordinated to the army at the time when they arrive at the location where combat operations are carried out, is resubordinated to the commander of armed forces, which is to say the military to the immediately Superior Commander? And at that point in time they enter the military hierarchy; is that correct or no?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they enter the military framework, the military hierarchy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please, item 8, last line reads: "In military operations, military rules and regulations shall be in force." This is linked to what we just described from item 7; is that correct or no?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. At the time when these MUP units are resubordinated to the army, all members of that unit lose the authorities they had as police officials, and they simply become ordinary plain members of the army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In that case, they held accountable under military rules as members of the army, and it is the military commander who is immediately responsible for them and their actions; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the platoon level it is the commander of the company and battalion that is responsible for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now, in that same item 8, it reads: "Any violation of regulations and failure to carry out tasks which have been ordered shall be subject to severe punishment and result in appropriate disciplinary and criminal punishment." Tell me, please, was that abided by in practice?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And now item 9 says that a staff shall be established and this staff is being established only in the structural sense, so to speak, and not in the sense of effective command and control; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I never received any kind of a letter signed by staff commander, so you are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever receive any sort of official letter from the police staff in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have information indicating that CSB that you belonged to, that [B/C/S spoken] or any other public security stations in your territory ever received any sort of letter sent by staff or staff commander?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that anybody received it. Under bullet 7, chiefs of CSB were also members of that staff, which means that had they received it in the hierarchical order, they were duty-bound to forward it further to the chiefs of public security stations, but no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krulj.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D46, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krulj, starting from the 1st of January 1991, you were appointed chief of the public security station in Ljubinje, the SJB in Ljubinje?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That appointment in 1991 was signed by minister of MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time, Mr. Alija Delimustafic, correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The proposal for your appointment to that post of the chief of SJB in Ljubinje came from your immediate superior, chief of CSB in Mostar; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Slobodan Bozic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krulj, you were not a member of the Serbian Democratic Party, were you?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Was it the Serbian Democratic Party that nominated you for this post, or was it your boss, chief of CSB in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the first multiparty elections, consultations in municipalities were carried out, consultations with presidents of municipalities, and the official proposal was normally written by chief of CSB. According to the then rules, and also rules later, members of MUP were not allowed to be members of any political parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Based on the territorial organisation that was in place, that was in force until 1992 within the Ministry of Interior, public security station in Ljubinje belonged to the CSB in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When the SAO Herzegovina was established, the territory of Ljubinje municipality became part of that regional community, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when SAO Herzegovina was established? If you cannot remember the date and month, do you at least know the year or what time of the year it was?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was in 1991, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement that you gave to the OTP, I can see that you were in Mostar for the last time on the 28th of March 1992, and that you visited precisely the CSB in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And on that day, there was an attack at the barracks in Mostar where a lot of people were killed and a lot of damage was caused by an explosive device?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And I suppose that this is why you remember that date so well?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I remember the date, yes, and a lot of these documents have become of age. It's been over 18 years since they were issued. But I remember that date because I sat with my colleagues at the CSB premises in Mostar and when I came home, I saw that a fire truck full of explosives was blown up next to the barracks. That's why I remember this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The attack was carried out by members of Croatian paramilitary formations; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It's likely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: From that day, from that date, is it actually then that the war broke out in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Mostar itself, yes. And as I've told you, within the borders of my municipality or at the borders of my municipality, it started a lot earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you something else. Do you remember the plan of the European Union on peaceful resolution of the situation in Bosnia from 1991 and 1992 which was popularly known as Cutileiro plan?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that. I remember that it existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that that plan envisaged mostly, in general terms, the division of Bosnia and Herzegovina into three entities, each of which would have its own organs including police and that in Sarajevo there would be the so-called federal ministries as they were known at the time?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that, it was quite frequently discussed at the time. I can't give you any details now, but it was quite a lot covered by the media. It received a lot of publicity, but then some changes came about and the plan was abandoned. At least that's what I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But you must remember that one of the key parts of that plan was the division of Bosnia into three entities, each of them with its own separate organs?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, anybody who is informed about general affairs knew about that. Anybody who was literate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And objectively this is very similar to the situation that was agreed on in Dayton in 1995, and on which the structure of Bosnia-Herzegovina for the past ten years is based; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krulj, can you please tell me, do you remember that the MUP minister of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Alija Delimustafic issued an order on the mobilisation of police reserves in September 1991? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, about the 20th of September, 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me the situation in the territory of your municipality and Bosnia and Herzegovina as a whole was very complex from the point of view of security because of the crisis and the war waging around Dubrovnik in 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the war was being waged some 20 kilometres or 10 kilometres as the crow flies from the centre of Trebinje. I mean, it was very close, that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me, there were members of the Yugoslav People's Army there, volunteers, as well as paramilitary forces; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me your opinion as a professional policeman, what was the discipline of those units like, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure if I'm being -- if I'm exaggerating, but I'm going to say it was terrible. They were creating terrible security problems for us. There was uncontrolled shooting around town, damage to vehicles, looting and robbery, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday during the examination-in-chief, in response to the Prosecutor's question relating to document P161, on page 49 of the transcript, line 13, you were answering a question that had to do with a paramilitary unit named Arkan's men, and my learned colleague was asking you about that. And then there was some problems about transcript entries, and I'm going to tell you the way I heard it and the transcript says differently. Can you please confirm. You said that vagabond, and I think you are thinking of some kind of tramp from the village, gathered some 30 people and formed some sort of unit that called itself Arkan's men, is that correct? And in the transcript what it said was that that man had said that he had killed 30 odd people, actually he gathered 30 people around him.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I thought I clarified that yesterday. Yes, that he assembled or gathered about him some 30 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read that from a document, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you read that from a document. That's right. Can you please tell me, all these armed groups, these volunteers, paramilitary forces members, army members, they were all in themselves more numerous than the police force in the area of your municipality?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were no such cases in my municipality. As for the other municipalities, there were some.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In the region of Herzegovina you are thinking?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, although we do have a station in Mostar which had some 15 members of the regular police force and volunteers, so these irregulars were much more numerous than the regular police officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And they were armed, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In the region of the whole area and your municipality, Ljubinje there was fear among the people?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. They were afraid and many of them were leaving. They were leaving for Serbia, for Montenegro. They were running away from the situation, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And this fear, of course, was related to the experiences of the Serbs in that area during World War II, and of course related to the situation that was leading to the conclusion that there would be a new war in the area?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, many information -- much information and misinformation was circulating, and there was -- in this area 2.000 casualties were the result of actions in 1941, and you can imagine how it was like, what those people felt when the Croatian forces appeared on the boundaries of the municipality. And then on the other side, a part of the Trebinje municipality was already occupied.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me, the check-points on the roads were set up during the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia's mandate; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military was there and there was some irregularity, so as soon as the reserve forces were mobilised, we set up check-points. Not just us, but it was pursuant to an order of the ministry of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So we set up check-points at all exits and entries to the municipality territory. We even received blue kiosks from the MUP urgently and we were instructed to set these up throughout the territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us the definition of a check-point briefly as part of the -- just one moment, can you just wait.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. A check-point is a permanent control or a check-point of the police manned continuously for 24 hours, meaning that all entrances and exits or passage of citizens is monitored. This is something that is conducted in peacetime. The check-point work is overseen by the Ministry of the Internal Affairs from Sarajevo, and this was done at that time as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Can you please tell me, you also had such oversight by Mr. Esad Rektic who was from the MUP and who came on behalf of Ejup Ganic from the ministry to check the work of the check-points?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were touring the area that was engulfed in war. His name was not Esad but Sead, from what I remember. He was the senior military officer and he was some sort of main inspector at the republican ministry. There was no such post at the republican Secretariat, but there was such a post in the republican Secretariat.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, the interpreters asked if you could be good enough to repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Okay, I'm sorry, I'm trying to move the speed further, I'm sorry, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In any event, this inspector general of the police who came to the area accompanied by Presidency member Ejup Ganic toured this check-point of yours and he didn't have any objections or any remarks; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me after the Law on Internal Affairs of Republika Srpska was adopted, there were changes in the territorial organisation and the Ljubinje SJB, where you were the chief, was then part of the security service of Trebinje territorially, which was actually formed under that law for the first time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your to date security centre was under the control of the Serbian forces; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me, Mr. Krsto Savic who was chief of the Trebinje CSB, before 1990, he worked in the police as assistant chief of police in Nevesinje; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was actually the assistant commander of the police in Nevesinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In 1989; is that correct, deputy commander?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in late 1989.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Then in 1990 he was promoted and became the chief of the public security station in Nevesinje; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And then he was appointed chief just like you were, the minister of the republican MUP of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Mr. Delimustafic -- Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mr. Delimustafic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me, 44 for the transcript, it's Mr. Alija Delimustafic. Can you please tell me, Mr. Krulj, the SAO Herzegovina after it was proclaimed formed its government, did it not?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Isn't it correct that that government had its minister of police, if I can put it that way and that position was occupied by Mr. Krsto Savic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So Mr. Krsto Savic as, let me put it that way, quote unquote, the minister of police of the SAO Herzegovina government, was in Trebinje practically before Republika Srpska was declared, before the constitution was adopted, the Law on Internal Affairs, and the MUP of Republika Srpska was formed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was. Mostly he was in Nevesinje but he was also in Trebinje. He didn't really come to see us all that much because at the time there was open combat in our area.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Krulj, could you just assist us in explaining in pursuit of the line of questioning that counsel is putting to you, how were the CSBs and the SJBs subordinated under the army during combat operations? How was that done, was that done by a written order to the chiefs of the SJBs and the CSBs, or was it just done informally or, can you explain the mechanism by which the police units were transferred and resubordinated to the armed forces? What was the mechanism that applied to this transfer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to explain it to you. I have a specific example from that time. At the time when the response to the call-up was not all that great and there weren't enough people to replenish the military forces, I was asked, and I did have the right under the law as chief of the station to lend out a unit of the police to a specific sector and a commander would be sent with those 25 people.
