And they were resubordinated to the second company of the military battalion that was holding that area. And this was regulated by law and I as the chief of the station of the police in Ljubinje had the right to engage a part of the police force in this manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I understand and thanks. But just how were you instructed or ordered to hand over this unit to the army? Was that by a written decision or by a telephone call from the commander of the 2nd Corps or whatever it was, the army officer? Just how did it happen? In other words, what I'm asking is that, is there any record of such transfers? Any requests made by the army to the police to resubordinate police units from the police to the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the municipality, we had the highest rank within the brigade, so the brigade commander asked us, commander of the brigade that had four battalions, so in order to replenish the Ljubinje battalion, he asked me to provide this assistance. The then Ministry of Bosnia and Herzegovina was aware of this type of help as well as the public security centre in Mostar because war was going on in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. We are talking about the 1st of October 1991. I'm now speaking about December, I'm not quite sure about the date now. This was quite a legitimate use of units of the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I'm not questioning the legitimacy. I think it was done probably according to the rules. My only interest was to understand better how it was done and when you, for instance, when you transferred a unit to the battalion, did you then receive a phone call from the commander of the battalion asking you to kindly resubordinate one of your units to him, or was it by virtue of a written order, or did the order come from the MUP? How was it done actually?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was done in such a way that by my decision on resubordination, the unit automatically becomes part of armed forces, and in a hierarchical sense they are responsible to the company commander and then the brigade commander. Once the reasons for their engagement no longer exist, I returned the unit back and I return it again to reserve forces. While the unit is within the military forces, they are not duty-bound to send any sort of reports to me, nor do I have any sort of duty with respect to them. I don't need to report them of anything because at that particular point in time they are no longer policemen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I understand. But what did you react upon? What triggered your decision to transfer one of your units to the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was informed about the security situation and I didn't have to be pushed to do this because a certain area had to be closed off. The decision had been taken at the meeting with the brigade commander. And I attended that meeting and I accepted to give some of my men to resubordinate them to them in order to close off the passage to that part of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well. So my question is, am I right in understanding that you went to a meeting where the commander of the brigade was attending and he asked around if any of the police chiefs could dispense with units and transfer them to him, and then you decided on your own authority to resubordinate one of your units to him immediately thereafter, is that how it happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue, Your Honours? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday during examination-in-chief, I think it remained unclear when my colleague on page 43, lines 12 to 18, you mentioned this Specijalna unit established by SAO Herzegovina in 1991 which was then sent to the Dubrovnik front. You said that this unit, in your view, comprised -- well, let me ask you this: Do you remember testifying about this yesterday?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that you said that this unit was not under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of the Interior, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You said that this unit was mostly manned by people who were on -- who were border-line criminals, I don't want to use too harsh words?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, it may have been too harsh a word but these people drove around in civilian vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This unit did not carry out any police tasks but rather participated only in combat operations and it didn't have any permanent establishment, rather when its participation in combat operation was needed, that unit would be assembled and sent to the front?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So this means that such a unit, this unit, was linked with the police only because somebody at some point in time gave this unit the name Specijalna unit of the police; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what they heard. They heard that something like that existed in the Knin Krajina and this is how they christened this unit, if I may say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So if I understand you well, this is a paramilitary unit that was organised; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, my municipality was the most endangered one, and they never came to my municipality, and nobody from my municipality was ever a member of that unit. And, yes, it could be said that it is a paramilitary unit because it did not belong to the regular police and it wasn't under the command of the military either.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Yesterday you tried to explain to the Trial Chamber and to the Prosecution something that I think is really important for this case and needs to be explained, so we have these paramilitary units that are called Specijalna units of the police without in essence having anything to do with the police, that's number one. And then we have the so-called Posebna police units which due to interpretation into English we can call PJP, Posebna units of police, PJP. Yesterday you explained how these units are established and what tasks they are assigned to, so could you now briefly repeat this to the Trial Chamber because I don't think that it was clearly entered into the transcript yesterday. So we are now dealing with PJP units, Posebna police units.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I will use this term PJP. In peacetime, in the peacetime organisation of the Ministry of the Interior, and I don't need to speak about responsibilities and jurisdiction now because I described that yesterday, so these units existed and they frequently had exercises both at the level of a police station and at the level of the security centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. I apologise, Mr. Krulj, but we don't want to be too broad about this. I want this to be explicit and clear. Let me try to guide you. You are much more experienced in these matters than I am, but I will do my best in order to make sure that it's clear for the Trial Chamber. So at the territory of each public security station, SJB, a certain number of acting policemen is selected, these are members of regular police force, and these people based on their mental and physical abilities are exceptional, right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And now these policemen from various public security stations at the level of a CSB are assembled and placed under the command of an inspector who is in charge of these matters within the CSB, and now these units are called Posebna police units, PJPs at the time?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I wanted to say that I was a commander of such a unit during an exercise in 1988 in Posusje, and I did this as a police inspector and we continued doing this later on as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now, these units, PJP units, were used for various purposes. For example, when there were football matches, such a PJP unit would be assembled, they would carry out the task of providing security during that football match, and following the completion of their tasks they would all go back to their original public security stations to carry out their regular duties?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So if we can summarise this, these PJP units exist only in order to carry out specific tasks, they are assembled and called to carry out that particular task, and upon the completion of that task, they are sent back to their regular duties within their own SJBs; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And now a third category in order to clarify this fully. There is a unit called Specijalna Brigade of the Ministry of the Interior, special brigade of the Ministry of Interior. So this Special Brigade is again a unit of the Ministry of the Interior, it's called a Special Brigade of MUP, and it existed back during the time of the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it was headquartered where, in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in Sarajevo, in Vrace, and in Krtelj which is a part of Sarajevo. It's not important where it was headquartered, but it existed within the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So that same type of unit, special brigade of MUP of Republika Srpska, was also established after the Law on Internal Affairs of Republika Srpska was passed, and that unit was under the command of Milenko Karisik; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This special brigade of MUP was also linked to the military at its seat, it was attached to the ministry at its seat, correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, solely there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: However, you spoke about the detachment of this unit, so the detachment of the special brigade of the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska under the command of Milenko Karisik sometime late in 1992, more likely in early 1993, so the detachment of that special brigade of MUP was created in the territory of the Trebinje CSB; is this correct what I just said?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Let me clarify. Let me explain briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Really briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right after the meeting in Belgrade, we had to find an area and ensure quality people for that unit. And at the time our manning strength was 40 per cent, that means that 40 per cent of our posts were occupied.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: And this is why it was delayed and it wasn't established until the end of the year or early 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So this detachment in essence had nothing to do with Trebinje CSB, this detachment of the special brigade, or with SJBs in that territory, it had nothing to do with them; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This detachment was directly linked, and it was under the command of the special brigade of MUP at the seat of the ministry, under the command of Milenko Karisik, correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now, I suppose that you know that these detachments of the special brigade in the territory of Trebinje were when needed and when so ordered by the commander of the MUP special brigade used to also carry out some Special Police tasks, complicated, complex tasks?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I hope that this explanation will be of assistance to the Trial Chamber and everybody else to understand this distinction between these three categories of units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Just one little question to clarify for me. If I remember well yesterday, and I'm talking now about a PJP units, the Posebna, and I think I remember that yesterday the witness told that this -- these units were in part reserve policemen commanded by active ones; is that correct? Do I remember that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: May the witness answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you answer?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the war, yes, they were also manned from reserve force. However, it was exclusively under the command of the police inspector from the police department at the centre, CSB, and that was that inspector's only job, only task.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, do you have any other questions about this because I would move on? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Krulj, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, I may have one problem, namely in relation to the information provided by Mr. Krulj relating to these paramilitary volunteer groups that seemingly were roaming around not being under the control of the police nor being under the control of the army, and my question is whether anyone actually tried to put these people under some sort of control?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You have heard the question, can you answer?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We tried our best and I managed to do that in my municipality because three or four men came to make some kind of unit that would be a kind of elite unit, so they asked for support. Some people who had a tendency to violate the law and they tended towards criminal acts and crimes and so on, but we prevented that. However, in some municipalities, and there were attempts like that in Trebinje, Nevesinje, Mostar, Gacko, we later engaged, because these units, these paramilitary units would come in 1993, 1994, so we tried through the ministry and the brigade to prevent this using our detachment. We had a little bit of help from the military police, but more or less we did manage to prevent it ourselves. I am not going to say that we were successful everywhere because it was not possible to do that, to go back to those times now it's difficult perhaps to explain that to you now. Perhaps I'm explaining to you things more from the aspect of a professional organisation, but actually out in the field you had armed men and mostly their objective was theft, and you are a policeman. I don't know if the answer is satisfactory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I realise that the situation must have been extremely difficult for everyone. Can I just ask for one clarification of your answer, namely, did you as head of the SJB try then to have these volunteer groups subordinated under your control, under the control of the police? Was that the aim, or what was the plan that you devised for bringing these volunteer groups under control?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I expelled them using my policemen. I expelled 13 people on the same day and there were none in my municipality. No paramilitary formations in my area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krulj, can you please tell me from late March when all this began in Mostar and you said that the attack on the barracks was carried out then, and then in the period that followed, yesterday you said that you had a lot of problems with roads and communication; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but yesterday when I was looking at a document, somebody asked me what the UKT connection was, and this was a connection via a hand-held device, and I saw that the Nevesinje communications proceeded through the centre for informing. And in the Stolac area it was done by messenger. And the Stolac area is in the 088 group, just like Ljubinje, so it used the relay station at Velis [phoen] so Ljubinje and Nevesinje have proper connections at the time. I saw that when the Prosecutor asked me about the meeting, she asked me about the UKT type of communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So if I understood you correctly, let me just summarise, the municipality of Ljubinje and the municipality of Nevesinje did have a telephone communication with Mostar, but at the time when the relay station was destroyed in Mostar through which all of these communications proceeded then the Ljubinje and Nevesinje municipalities were cut off and left without any telephone lines or communication; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I remember correctly you said yesterday that this lasted for some four or five months or longer until another relay station was set up at Leotar, I think, mount Leotar; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This happened sometime between the 10th and the 20th of May, that's when the relay was knocked down, at Velis. I don't know how long, how many months it to took them to make this new one. I really cannot tell. But in any case, it took at least three or four months, maybe more.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just one more question about this particular situation at the time. You said yesterday during your examination-in-chief that the public security station in Ljubinje before war began, sometime in March or April and May 1992, operated -- actually, that a lady, a Muslim woman worked there at the public security station; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, she was working on issuing identification papers and car registration.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And throughout the whole wartime period, she stayed on the same job and if I remember correctly, you said that she was still working on the same job today; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did anyone ever pressure you since you were the chief of the public security station to remove that lady from service or to fire her or anything like that, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness now be shown document 65 ter 47. 65 ter number 47.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's already exhibited by me.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P158.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Actually can we see P158, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is in your tab 2, information on the work of the Trebinje CSB in the period of 1st of July until the 15th of August; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You were shown the document by the Prosecutor yesterday. I would just very briefly like to look at page 2, paragraph 3. I think that it's the same thing in the English. Yes, in English it's paragraph 4 from the top. Actually, it's on page 3, I apologise. Madam Korner criticised Mr. O'Donnell yesterday because of the stamps, and I just have to do the same thing myself, now. Paragraph 4 beginning with the words "a special problem," do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In that report, just like you mentioned before, you said that you pointed out problems of the non-functioning of the communication system and other problems that you encountered; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. We are going to move to the next document. We also need to pay attention to the time. Can you please tell me -- Your Honours, I'm being warned that it's time for a break perhaps?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I think we have another 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, yes, I will continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] we resume at 5.40. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if it pleases the Court, can I have the document on the e-court while we wait for the witness, in order to save time? Can I call P160, please. I need page 13 in Serbian, and page 16 in English. This is a good page in English, but the Serbian page another three pages, this is number 10 and I need 13, one three. I'm sorry? I'm sorry, I'm sorry, I don't know the -- next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. That's perfect. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: While the witness is taking his position, Mr. Zecevic, I'd remind you, you have 55 minutes remaining.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I know, Your Honours, I was just discussing with the Registry, I might ask for a leave to -- because I have a lot of documents which I need -- which I would need some time to present with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I will try my best to speed it up as much as I can, Your Honours. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krulj, yesterday the Prosecutor showed you P160 which are the minutes from the first collegium of the MUP of the Republika Srpska. I think this is tab 3, and it's dated the 11th of July, 1992 in Belgrade. I think it's open at the correct document. Can you please tell me, isn't it correct that the collegium meeting, the first one was held in Belgrade in July of that year because that was the only place where all the chiefs of the CSBs from the territory of Republika Srpska could come together?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because we all went through Montenegro or Serbia when we were going to Bijeljina or Pale. I didn't go to Sarajevo then because the road was even longer through Vlasenica, Sekovici, it was some 700 kilometres actually to get there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall that in August a collegium session was held in Trebinje and Mr. Zupljanin -- or the Banja Luka CSB were unable to attend because Mr. Zupljanin was not able to come; do you recall speaking about that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I actually saw that from the diary who was present and he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at page 13 now. It's already on the screen.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I need to look at the paragraph that begins with the words "otherwise." I'm just going to read it to you, and I'm going to put one question on it to you. This is the text spoken by Mr. Mico Stanisic the minister. He says: "... the basic thing from which we will not retreat" -- in the English text, I apologise, it is -- it's the first paragraph on page 16 of the English. "... the basic thing from which we will not back away from is that the MUP is a professional organisation, a professional police force, not influenced by politics, which means no individuals, groups, different currents or parties influence it. After all, the Presidency of the Serb republic passed a decision forbidding party action in a war regime. This means that our work is professional from the jurisdiction of Internal Affairs organs aimed at creating state with rule of law, and making it functional." You as the chief of the public security station, did you abide by these professionalism guide-lines and apply them to the members of the police force at your public security station?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. On page 14 in the B/C/S and then on the English page, we have the correct page, it's page 16 in the Serbian text this is on page 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's one paragraph but last, and I'm going to read it to you. It's also something that Mr. Stanisic said: "In order to achieve full constitutionality and legality and in order to implement the other legal acts, we have decided to prevent criminal acts not only by civilians, but also those committed by soldiers and members of the army by active and reserve policemen and members of Internal Affairs organs and their superiors for whom it is established that they committed any type of criminal offence." Can you please tell me if you abided by these guide-lines by the minister of police, Mr. Stanisic, in the course of 1992?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'm going to ask you to look at the conclusions. This is on page 20 of the B/C/S text and in the English it's on page 21. And we will look at paragraph marked with the number 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We just need to look at one page later in the Serbian. The English page is all right but the text in Serbian is not on the correct page. The document page is page 20 and so I'm not really able to tell you the page number in e-court. All right, thank you, it's okay now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And you can see on the basis of all the discussion, conclusion number 1 is here. Earlier we looked at this diary and you said and you pointed out in response to a question by my learned friend that a meeting held after the collegium, all the 18 conclusions were presented to all the public security station representatives in the region; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please tell me, in conclusion number 1, in the last sentence it says: "The priorities before us spring from the conclusions that follow, and above all, they include gathering information on activities of the enemy, on war crimes, on serious forms of criminal offences, especially looting and war profiteering, et cetera." Tell me, please, did you consider this to be a mandatory conclusion, and did you also consider this to be a priority in your work?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that each professional policeman considered this to be a priority.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now skip three pages forward in the Serbian, and then in the English text it will be page 24. Item 7, yes, we have the good page in the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let us now go over this quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see item 6. Could the witness see item 6 too, in the English text as well. It's on the same page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You can see here that item 6 pertains to prevention and documenting of war crimes, and it speaks of that; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now would you please look at item 7, it says: "Prevention and detection of other crimes and their perpetrators with priorities being looting, war profiteering, aggravated criminal offences against somebody's life and limb and other criminal offences regardless of who the perpetrators are." Did you uphold these conclusions in your work regardless of who the perpetrators were?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his answer because they were overlapping question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Would you please repeat the second part of your answer because it wasn't recorded, and please speak up.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As regards this paragraph where it says that those responsible to carry out these tasks, they list CSBs, SJBs, and the administration for the affairs and tasks of the crime prevention department.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. See this in item 6 there is something that I would like to comment with you. Item 6 under the conclusion speaks of documenting war crimes committed by the enemy. Do you see it? Do you see the text? Yesterday the Prosecutor showed you a criminal report signed by you, P167, and that was in 1994. You filed that criminal report, that criminal complaint in relation -- against members of Muslim forces from the territory of Capljina for crimes committed against Serbs in that municipality in 1992. Do you remember that document?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In order not to waste time, tell me, please, Capljina is a neighbouring municipality, right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stolac municipality is in between our municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And how far is it from your municipality?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: 43 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Capljina was not within the territory of Republika Srpska, was it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I suppose it means that it was outside of the territorial jurisdiction of the Trebinje CSB?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, you investigated these crimes committed against Serbs in the territory of municipality which was under the control of Muslim forces because, I suppose, there were some doubts whether that would be documented under the territory which was under their control; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: To be fully fair, even had they wanted to conduct an investigation and to file charges for those war crimes, they were faced with an objective problem because all of the witnesses and victims were in the territory of Republika Srpska. You spoke about that yesterday saying that some of them were even as far away as in Bijeljina and that you had to look for them?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in Bijeljina, in Serbia, and some of them even abroad in America and western Europe.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I mean, this created real difficulties for employees of the Ministry of the Interior on both sides, this fact that neither witnesses nor victims were available to them, they had no access to them, so they couldn't really conduct an investigation in accordance with the regulations and rules of the profession?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I suppose that the MUP of Republika Srpska had identical problems in documenting war crimes committed against some other ethnic groups in the territory of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The document that we just saw, the collegium of the 11th of July 1992 in Belgrade, there was some discussion about problems caused by the non-functioning of the military judiciary, do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: There was also some discussion about the non-functioning of civilian courts in the largest part of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in our territory, yes. Non-functioning which went over a long period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let's explain that. When you say in your territory, you mean the territory of the Trebinje CSB, that is to say, the territory of Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So in the territory of Herzegovina, the judiciary and other judicial organs didn't function properly?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time there was just the basic court which at the time was known as the municipal court in Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. We are now dealing with 1992, say from April until the end of the year; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, you are going by all means too fast. I'm going to slow down by putting a question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC ASKED YOU
utterances.text: "I suppose that the MUP or that the MUP of Republika Srpska had identical problems in documenting war crimes committed against some other ethnic groups in the territory of the Republika Srpska?" Answer: "Yes." I don't really get the sense of the question and the sense of the answer, what do you mean by your yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I meant to say is that I meant that it was linked to the previous question, that in relation to the criminal report that I signed, it was difficult for the police of the Federation to collect documents about those crimes committed because there were no witnesses. All of the witnesses were either in the territory of Republika Srpska or abroad. Similar problems were encountered by the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska also because they couldn't locate witnesses when it comes about -- when it comes to Bosniaks, and they also couldn't locate, say, members of paramilitary units. And both sides encountered such problems in documenting these war crimes. That's what I spoke about, or maybe I misunderstood the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: No, no, probably not. And then you mean you had problems in the Republika Srpska in relation to crimes committed in the Republika Srpska? That's what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just briefly, to clarify, I hope I will be of assistance to the Trial Chamber and you as well. So when we speak of these crimes, say a crime is committed, victims and witnesses usually after the crime cross over into the territory which is under the control of Muslim or Croat forces, and by doing so they make it impossible for you to carry out an investigation, to file a criminal report, to locate people who would testify, and they make it impossible for you to collect key evidence necessary in order to institute criminal proceedings against the perpetrators? You cannot find witnesses to identify perpetrators, that's the essence of the problems?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's how I understood it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And the same applied to the members of the MUP from Muslim and Croat parts that were under the control of Muslim and Croat forces because their witnesses would also cross over into the territory of Republika Srpska or go to other countries throughout the world?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope the Trial Chamber is satisfied or if you need me, I can put additional questions about this to the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now, let us go back to the judicial organs. The previous territorial organisation of judicial organs of Bosnia and Herzegovina had the district court in Mostar as the highest court for the entire territory of Herzegovina; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In the territory of Herzegovina parts of which was Republika Srpska, there was just one basic court and it was located in Trebinje?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: After Republika Srpska was established and its judicial organs, a higher court in Trebinje was set up and there also remained the basic courts in Trebinje, and the third court was set up in Nevesinje; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In that situation this establishment and the setting up of courts went very slowly and it wasn't very efficient; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In comparison with the peacetime when you compare the function of courts during peacetime to the situation that existed in the greater part of 1992, could you say that the judicial system when it comes to criminal proceedings functioned properly or not?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it functioned at the time. I think that there were only two judges in the basic court in Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This absolutely did not mean that the police did not carry out on-site investigations in every single case and all the other investigative measures with criminal reports as a result, regardless of the fact that the courts were not functioning at the time?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So your competencies and your tasks were completed when US police filed a criminal report with the relevant responsible Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, unless certain additional investigative measures are requested.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You said that before the war you went out to inspect public security stations throughout Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, all of them. All of them Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So, yes, throughout Herzegovina before the war, say starting in 1986, and in 1989, and in 1990 and so on?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sure that you know that every public security station has something that is called a KU registry book?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in their crime prevention section.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you, but very briefly, please, explain to us what this KU register contains, what kind of information?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the police station there are several important registers or books. One is the book of daily events which is kept by the duty service of the police. They enter into this book all of the events, all of the reports that come in from citizens, and all of the crimes. In addition to this, in the crime prevention police there is also a book which is permanently archived and it is known as a K register, which is the register of crimes. So crimes are recorded in two books. Information there entered concerns a perpetrator whether he is known or not known when the investigation was commenced, when it was concluded, and so on, so for each crime there are several columns over two pages, over 15 columns for each entry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you said that this K register is a permanent document?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That means that in the public security station, this document is held in perpetuity?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So each station is obliged to preserve this document?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me whether this register was maintained for each year separately or it was maintained continuously? For example, was a register started when the station was opened, and then maintained until the book was full when a new one would be started? Can you explain how it worked?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, on the 31st of December of each year one K register would be completed. It would be closed. There would be a stamp placed, and it would be signed by the chief of the station or a police official, and then a new one would be started for the next year until the book was spent.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now that we are discussing this matter, yesterday on page 34, line 6 to 15 you were asked by my learned friend from the Prosecution about the planting of explosives at the mosque in Ljubinje; do you remember that from yesterday?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me, this specific incident by its very nature and according to the nature of police work, it should be entered into the daily event log-book; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: After that a team would be sent to the crime scene?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: An investigation would be conducted. Did you speak with any witnesses?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that we did. I don't know how much I would need to explain that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, I'm just asking you about the system, the way things work.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So all the documents are held in a police file; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And each of those actions would be documented in the K register; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The act is recorded, not each supplemental action or document that goes into the file. You could have 50 documents, 50 statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Very well. You told us yesterday that you didn't manage to find the perpetrators of that crime?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And so is this crime registered as committed by unidentified perpetrators in the register?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And criminal charges was submitted against unidentified perpetrators; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can answer the way the procedures officially were supposed to be conducted, but, yes, that is how it's usually done.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In that particular instance and in other cases, all the data in the K registers in all the stations still exist, right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is how the police force works. It's not something that is out of the ordinary. Everybody knows that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Isn't it also correct that the key document in your work are the rules on the execution of duties in the police force?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This rule book existed at the Ministry of Internal Affairs of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, do you remember from what year?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was after the law. This is a kind of rule book with guide-lines that is adopted after the law is passed, guiding the work of the police force. So it dates from 1977. If any new rules are adopted or such guide-lines, mostly they are copied from somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me the rules of the MUP, of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina from 1977 was used after the MUP of Republika Srpska was formed in 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: After the MUP of Republika Srpska rules were adopted on the execution of duties in the domain of public security, it's identical to this one, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, until the new Law on Criminal Procedure was adopted when the times that one is allowed to stay in official premises was changed. In the rule book this was changed to three days, and it's slightly different in the law, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me the Law on Criminal Procedure that you just referred to which influenced and had the effect of changes in the rules, when was it adopted?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Perhaps in 2003 or 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can you please tell me just one thing, we talked about that. Actually, you covered that with the Prosecutor yesterday. The collegium in July 1992, you said in your statements, and I think also yesterday you mentioned it, that the minister, Mr. Stanisic and his associates wanted you as a professional policeman with considerably more experience than Krsto Savic take over the leadership of the Trebinje CSB?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not like that. They wanted me to come to Trebinje and to perform the duties of a deputy. I don't know if the minister wanted that exactly, but I was often called because of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The Ministry of Republika Srpska in the course of 1992 sent certain Working Groups for the purpose of improving the situation in the Trebinje CSB, do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday during the examination-in-chief you looked at a document dated the 6th of July, it was a meeting of the 6th of July, 1992, attended by Mr. Skipina and some other members of the MUP of Republika Srpska from the headquarters who had come to attend this kind of meeting; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me during such meetings which were attended by such Working Groups or kind of inspection, did they criticise the state of affairs and did they seek that improvements be made and that work be done strictly according to the law, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I would now like to show you some documents and orders of some gentlemen from the ministry and from Mr. Stanisic, and perhaps we can comment on them to see which documents you received and which ones you are familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at document 1D2751, please. I think that that is the fifth tab, tab 5 in your set of documents.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just while that's being done, I spoke to Mr. Zecevic about these documents before and asked him where they had been obtained from. These aren't our documents, I don't think. And I'd just like to clarify for the record that they were acquired by the Defence from the RS MUP. Is that right, Mr. Zecevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You opened the document, it's an order to public security stations dated the 26th of July. It should be in your tab 5.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tab 6 actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tab 6, all right, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at the document. It's a document from the Security Services Centre in Trebinje, which I hope was delivered to you as well. Do you recall that document?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The document conveys an order by the minister of Internal Affairs, or the Ministry of Internal Affairs, based on the conclusions that we reviewed, the ones from the first ministry collegium session of the 11th of July held in Belgrade, and some previous and some subsequent ministry documents. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When we look at Article 1, it says: "All MUP members who committed crimes with the exception of political and verbal offences prior to or since the beginning of combat activities or the establishment of the MUP of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, take legal measures to remove them from our ranks, relieve them of duty, and place them at the disposal of the Army of Republika Srpska." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me -- actually, let us comment on this a little bit because the fact is being sort of mystified here in this case. When the ministry insists in this way for certain individuals to be removed because they do not deserve to be members of the MUP because of their previous activities, this is one aspect of it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The other aspect is that while they were members of the MUP from the beginning of the combat activities and the establishment of the MUP, they had committed some criminal acts so this is the second option for removal; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that a such persons who committed certain crimes are being pardoned and that criminal proceedings are not conducted against them or not?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not a pardon. Criminal charges or misdemeanour charges are submitted against those persons. The second category is the combat assignment if we are talking about active members of the force. That person is being transferred to the Army of Republika Srpska as a wartime assignment, and against them criminal charges will be submitted, and this is something that I did as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. We will have examples, but let us clarify this first. This means that, for example, a member of the police force carries out a crime. At the time when information is discovered that this person had committed a crime, actions are taken in respect of that person just like they would be taken in respect of any other person.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: So if a person is a police officer, they are supposed to prevent somebody else from stealing, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, for the purposes of my question and the transcript, please answer yes or no, so what is the answer?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So investigation is initiated against such a person which will perhaps result in criminal charges being submitted and then that person would be placed under the jurisdiction of the Prosecutor's Office for further processing; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In case we are talking about a more serious crime, a more serious crime, the perpetrator is arrested and detained up to a period of three days; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mentioned for the transcript would be detained for a period of up to three days. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So these proceedings are conducted in relation to any person regardless of whether they are a member of the MUP or not?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In the event that we are talking about a crime that does not require detention or arrest of a person, that person who committed such a crime is subject to disciplinary proceedings within the ministry or within your public security station; is that correct? And this person's disciplinary responsibility is different from his criminal responsibility?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So this means that the disciplinary responsibility remains within the public security station, whereas criminal responsibility is forwarded on to the Prosecutor and the Court for further action; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So in the cases where we have a perpetrator of a minor crime, which does not require that that person be arrested or put into custody, such a MUP member is suspended by the ministry, a criminal report is filed against that person to the responsible Prosecutor, and at that moment, this person is placed at the disposal of the armed forces of Republika Srpska; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So this is the meaning of this order, that this is what needs to be done rather, it doesn't mean that somebody is pardoned in relation to a crime that that person has committed; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In accordance with the then --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I ask you, are you asking me whether the only punishment for a crime is being sent to the army?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well ...

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose you know that that's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I know that, but we are hearing different kinds of arguments here. But tell me, based on our then regulation and also now, regulations now in existence, it is only the president who has a right to pardon somebody from criminal prosecution according to the constitution; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, this need to place such persons and all other persons at the disposal of the Army of Republika Srpska stemmed from the pressure that you as members of police faced from the citizens and members of the Army of Republika Srpska in relation to your reserve force; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: At the time it was believed that if somebody is a member of police reserve force, that was an avenue for evading going to the front and taking part in combat activities there, that was one of the ways of evading it; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And then all of these civilian organs and the military pressured you to transfer these police reserve members to the military reserve and have them sent to the front; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In addition to that, the actual situation at the front was such that they always lacked personnel who was fit for the military?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So in the context that we have explained just now, that is the context in which we need to read this order that we have just discussed?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I tender this order in evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D47, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, when I asked you about this order you said that you had a case in your career where you disciplined one of your workers and placed him under -- at the disposal of the Army of Republika Srpska, can you explain?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, briefly. Not just one. I disciplined more than one. There were several suspensions, but if you suspend such a worker and he stays at home just lying there and there's a war going on, and I have a case of a policeman who drove somebody while under the influence. They went to a village, they got drunk there, and this policeman was then in a traffic accident in which the vehicle was completely destroyed. So naturally, I filed a criminal report against that policeman. I suspended him, I submitted a claim for compensation in the amount of the value of the vehicle. He was suspended, and then transferred to the Army of Republika Srpska. And when it comes to misdemeanours where say somebody stole 5 litres of fuel from an official car, well, we didn't have just a single such case, we had more.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember the name of this policeman of yours that was prosecuted?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nenad Popara.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we have a date, if that's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when that was? Do you remember the date?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was in the summer of 1992. I'm not sure about the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Is this satisfactory for you? Summer of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's the best we should have.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, I shouldn't have interrupted in any event, but I was just wondering if he could give us a date, that was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I've said to you, I will be putting some other documents to you from the MUP of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown 1D693, which should be the following document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is a document or rather a dispatch dated 17th December 1992. It was sent by the MUP administration at its seat to all chiefs of SCBs [as interpreted] and all chiefs of SJBs, do you remember this document, you should have received it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was a cable which was the usual type of communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So this cable again pertains to checks of all MUP employees through operative misdemeanours and criminal records; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In addition to order -- to the order which stipulated that those who had a negative record had to be relieved of duties immediately, and there was also a punishment envisioned in such cases?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It says here that payment of wages would be stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we tender -- could we have a number for this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: It's now admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D48, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown 65 ter 261, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is an order of the Ministry of the Interior from Bijeljina number 52/92, dated 23rd October 1992, and again it was sent to all chiefs of CSB and SJBs, and in it they order the redaction of the reserve police force, and it also says that the remaining reserve policemen have to be made available for wartime assignment in the Army of Republika Srpska. Do you remember this document?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And perhaps we initiated such a document for the well known problems that they always asked us to do this. And it says here that all military commands be notified that we are no longer duty-bound to provide policemen to send them to the front. It was a very big problem for us, and I think that in a meeting we initiated this. We started this initiative. We asked the minister to act, or rather, we highlighted this problem for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This order, if I understood you well, should be put in the context with what we spoke about earlier where there was pressure on the part of civilian authorities and the militaries to send reserve policemen to the front, that was on one side, and on the other side in cases where policemen were resubordinated to the military, the military would take away your personnel that you needed in order to carry out your police tasks; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Which means that they made it impossible for you to carry out the tasks for which the police was established, the police is meant to carry out these tasks?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And this is why you asked that such an order be issued. You initiated this?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we couldn't ask for an order to be issued, but we highlighted this as a problem. And it didn't only exist in our territory. It existed in most other locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In addition to legislation and rules in the police, you are also duty-bound to act in accordance with mandatory instructions; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those are sublaws regulating the work of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we tender this into evidence, please. This document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D49.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown 1D00-4279, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Just to correct the transcript, the exhibit that has just been admitted is 1D49.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, this is a document of the Ministry of the Interior dated 28th September 1992. This is the document of Republika Srpska, of course, and these are instructions on the rules of behaviour and interpersonal relations of the personnel of the Ministry of the Interior. Do you see this?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did you receive this instruction?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and we had some similar before the war. This is a code of behaviour for the Ministry of Interior workers, and I think it's similar or perhaps even identical to the one before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So these instructions specify rules of behaviour and also rules for interpersonal relations among the members of the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And that's very important in order to establish order within the ministry?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR KRULJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we also have this document exhibited, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D50.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown -- just a moment, please. 1D2436.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Again instructions, and I think that you mentioned it yesterday --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, we were wondering whether in the interest of being as economical with time as we could, if your -- the documents which you are now seeking to tender all tend towards the same point, seek to establish the same point, whether -- subject of course to what the Prosecution has to say, they couldn't be tendered together rather than -- because of the four that you have -- that this witness has been -- tendered through this witness, they are -- whereas they are different in their specifics, they all tend to go to establish system so --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, let me -- if I may interrupt you, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I don't have anything against that. These are the orders of the Ministry of Interior of Republika Srpska, some instructions, some documents which are all official documents. I gave the other binder to the witness if the witness can have the binder over night maybe he can check out and we can give them the numbers according to the list which I provided to all parties, and they may be admitted as exhibits, if my learned friend does not object to that. And that would significantly shorten the period. Your Honours, I do intend to rely on these documents. It's either -- I think this is -- these are obviously very important documents. Many of them are signed by Mr. Stanisic himself. Therefore, we do intend to rely on these documents. Either we introduce them through this witness or any other, it's...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I think, if I may interrupt, the point that was suggested by the presiding judge was simpler, namely, to simply ask if any of these documents could be grouped together for the purpose of showing one part only. Like, if the issue is that you wish to show that instructions were handed out from various authorities for the purpose of imposing discipline on the police personnel or MUP personnel, then perhaps those could be grouped together and just put in as one bundle. And then we could admitted those four or five documents together in one rather than having to go through each of them because we can't see from your list what these documents are about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand. I know. Your Honour, I can do that. The only problem is, for example, we have I believe three or four instructions which are obviously documents which as the witness said were essential for the operation of the -- daily operation of the MUP. They are only instructions, but they refer to different -- different matters. That's why I'm concerned if we give -- maybe we can give one number like 100 A, B, C or 1 or something. I am perfectly willing to accommodate the Trial Chamber with that. Because we are anyhow finishing now, I can do that overnight and come up with solution as I can in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, you have overnight to think about how you would approach this, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, I will.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If it assists, as far as documents are concerned that appear on the face of it to be signed or sent on behalf of Mico Stanisic and on the basis of the assurance I receive from counsel that these were obtained by the Defence from the RS MUP, and obviously I'm not going to object to them going in, I mean, for whatever reason we haven't got these documents, some of them anyhow. So on that basis, however he chooses to deal with it is all right with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thanks. It's just that the same rule applies to the Defence that applies to the Prosecution, namely that the Chamber needs to at least be given some idea about what these documents contain.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, I understand. I intend to ask the witness, but, Your Honours, it can be simple. I can list down the instructions and I can ask him, Are these instructions the instructions that you received in 1992, have you followed these instructions, and that's -- I think that would be it. And the witness can have the binder tonight in order to reflect his memory. Thank you very much. Shall we --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As we've got two minutes left can I just raise tomorrow with Your Honours, which -- the next witness rather?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: He should be excused.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, the witness can leave. Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krulj, you are still -- as you would appreciate, I'm certain, your evidence is still not complete, and I would remind you of the instructions that I gave you yesterday, that during the overnight adjournment, you can't speak with counsel from either side and in your discussions with anyone outside the Chamber you can't discuss your testimony. So we would resume tomorrow morning at 9.00 in this courtroom. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, again you may have gathered from what Mr. Zecevic has proposed, you would be left a bundle overnight that you can peruse and see whether some of the documents in that once you were to familiarise yourself with them, are documents which are of the same class and character that can go in together, but it would be counsel's call. When you return tomorrow, you would be in a position to answer counsel's question in that regard. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am aware this document, these are instructions and orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So you may have the binder overnight to familiarise yourself with them. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Trial Chamber and legal officer confer]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just wanted to confirm that Your Honours' order as to how I deal with the evidence that -- the documents that Mr. Djeric can deal with stands and therefore I can make a selection from the categories, and the rest will be -- no, the rest will be MFI'd subject to cross-examination, is that still the order? All right. Well, leaving that aside, Your Honour, we are coming to intercepts tomorrow. I thought there was only one. In fact, a check has revealed that there are no less than seven altogether -- one extra one but on top of the one, which Mr. Djeric has to listen to. Now, he has already listened to one, and I've told Mr. Zecevic this, he has identified the voice of the speaker and to the extent he can recognise his own voice, his voice. The whole question of intercepts is now outstanding we have responded today five days earlier than we ought but we have actually filed the response today. My understanding from Mr. Zecevic, however, is if Mr. Mr. Djeric can say yes I recognise the voice of the other person to whom I'm speaking, I can lead that evidence. Is that right? I just want to make sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, I said -- it was a misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, then I don't where we are going to. That's going to be a problem tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We are obviously.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I know it's time but we'll have to because as I say, there are seven intercepts which I want to deal with and how we deal with it when the motion was served a week ago or ten days ago, I don't know, but I'm going to be arguing that I should be allowed to lead that evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It was my understanding that Your Honours wanted to rise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes, but we are again stressing the interpreters and it is something that we cannot and should not do. But, Ms. Korner is asking for an indication from the Chamber here now, so if you can put down your comments very very quickly then we'll be able to rule on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, we objected to the intercepts. There is a motion pending. That is our position. I talked to Ms. Korner today. In a situation where the witness would be able to say, okay, this is my conversation with this person, I recognise my voice, of course, and it this person's voice, of course. Then our objection will only be limited to -- not to the authenticity, but to the actual legality of the intercept because we have -- I don't know if you read our motion, there is two or three points why we are objecting against the intercepts. So that is the essence of our communication. But doesn't mean -- I just want to put this on the record, Your Honour. It doesn't mean that somebody else can come and say oh, yes, I recognise, I talked to Mr. Zecevic years ago and Mr. Cvijetic and I know this is -- those are the two voices. That will not go. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I thank the interpreters for their indulgence, and we take the adjournment now until tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 28th day of October, 2009, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.04 p.m.
